title: Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability
claim: The added interpretability module costs a tiny fraction of the base model's compute, so the overhead is negligible.
layout: single horizontal bar chart, three bars, value labels at bar ends
description: A single horizontal bar chart with three bars on a white background with light vertical gridlines. The x-axis is 'Time per 1M tokens (s)', running from 0 to 200. The bars are all solid blue. The top bar, 'LLM forward', is very long at 196.8 s, and its label sits inside the bar in white. Below it, 'SASA forward' is a tiny sliver at 3.3 s, and 'SASA backward' is a similar sliver at 4.6 s. Both have dark labels just to the right of the bar. The eye goes first to the long top bar, then to the contrast with the two short bars. The figure shows that SASA's computational overhead is small compared with the base LLM's forward pass. It does not show the concept geometry, PCA rings, or SAE-versus-SASA latent bars that the caption describes.
caption: Concept geometry and feature splitting in Mistral-7B. At the top, PCA projections of layer-8 activations show rings and curves, with days and months centered within each carrier sentence. Interventions along the circular representations of days and months change calendar predictions, while movement along the age curve favors "senior" over "child". At the bottom left, colors identify the $12$ SAE latents [ref] and $2$ SASA groups with the dominant contributions to the representation of months. The bars show $77$ SAE latents and $8$ SASA groups selected for their responses to month-name tokens (Appendix [ref]). Within these sets, the colored units contribute $28%$ of SAE activations and $67%$ of SASA group $\ell_2$ norms over month-name tokens. The monthly centroids within the dominant SASA group form a complete ring in calendar order (right).
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used for mechanistic interpretability in large language models, yet their standard formulation assigns each latent feature a single decoder direction, implicitly assuming features to be one-dimensional. We show that this assumption can induce feature splitting when model features are multi-dimensional. Geometrically, accurately reconstructing a feature under a fixed co-activation budget can require exponentially many decoder directions as its dimension grows. From an optimization perspective, adding decoder directions can strictly lower the $\ell_1$-regularized population risk, even when a basis can already reconstruct the feature exactly. Motivated by these results, we introduce Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders (SASA), which replace single-vector decoders with learned subspaces, enforce sparsity through Top-$s$ group gating, and adapt group rank with nuclear-norm regularization. Under an idealized single-feature model, we prove that the SASA objective is minimized by a single group whose reconstruction map recovers the feature subspace. We also derive polynomial sample complexity bounds for subspace estimation within a group and a lower bound on the samples needed to observe every atom in a fixed fragmented dictionary. Experiments on GPT-2 and Mistral-7B show reduced absorption compared with SAEs. Matched-budget GPT-2 comparisons show lower absorption for concept families and more accurate prediction of their members using a small number of latent coordinates, at a reconstruction cost. The code is available at https://github.com/arshandalili/sasa.
